passage: Light behaves in predictable ways when it interacts with different materials. When light travels from one transparent medium to another, it changes speed, causing it to bend specifically at the boundary between the two media. This bending, known as refraction, occurs regardless of whether the medium is a liquid, gas, or solid. When we use lenses, the light rays do not stop at the image location; instead, they continue traveling through space, allowing us to see the image from different angles. A concave lens always produces a virtual, diminished image, regardless of the object's distance, because it diverges light rays. In contrast, the power of a lens is inversely proportional to its focal length, meaning a lens that bends light more sharply has a shorter focal length and higher power. Furthermore, when we look at a mirror, the image is not physically located on the glass surface itself, but appears to be behind it due to the reflection of light rays. Finally, magnification tells us about the image size and orientation; a negative magnification value indicates that the image is inverted, but it does not necessarily mean the image is smaller than the object.

items.evidence: When light travels from one transparent medium to another, it changes speed, causing it to bend specifically at the boundary between the two media.
items.q: A ray passes from air into a glass block. Where exactly does its path change direction?
options: Right at the surface where air meets glass
Gradually, as it moves deeper into the glass
Only at the far side where it leaves
Nowhere, because glass is not a liquid
items.explain: Light changes speed and bends at the boundary between two media, and this happens in solids too.

wrong.why: thinks light bends inside the second medium
thinks bending happens only when light leaves
thinks light refracts only in liquids

items.evidence: When we use lenses, the light rays do not stop at the image location; instead, they continue traveling through space, allowing us to see the image from different angles.
items.q: Why can people standing at different angles all see the image made by a lens?
options: The rays keep going past the image point
The rays stop at the image and light it up
The rays form the image on the lens surface
The rays bounce back from the image to us
items.explain: Rays do not stop at the image; they keep travelling, so it can be seen from many angles.

wrong.why: thinks rays stop where the image forms
thinks the image sits on the surface
mixes up refraction by lenses with reflection

items.evidence: A concave lens always produces a virtual, diminished image, regardless of the object's distance, because it diverges light rays.
items.q: A candle is placed very far from a concave lens. What kind of image forms?
options: Virtual and smaller than the candle
Real and smaller, as it is far away
Virtual and larger than the candle
Real and inverted on a screen
items.explain: A concave lens spreads rays apart, so its image is always virtual and smaller, at any distance.

wrong.why: thinks a far object gives a real image
mixes up concave and convex lenses

items.evidence: In contrast, the power of a lens is inversely proportional to its focal length, meaning a lens that bends light more sharply has a shorter focal length and higher power.
items.q: Lens A has a higher power than lens B. How does lens A compare with lens B?
options: It has a shorter focal length
It has a longer focal length
It has the same focal length
It has weaker bending of light
items.explain: Power is inversely related to focal length, so higher power means shorter focal length and sharper bending.

wrong.why: thinks higher power means longer focal length
thinks power does not depend on focal length
reverses the link between power and bending
